items: Repo name must be `terraform-<PROVIDER>-<NAME>`
Semver Git tags required — the registry needs both
`README.md` becomes the registry landing page

blocks.title: Deprecation Path
blocks.text: Keep the old variable, mark it deprecated in `description`, `coalesce` it with the new one, delete only at the next major.

items: One module = one logical unit of infrastructure
Cannot name it in three words? It is two modules
Name the single primary resource `this`: `aws_vpc.this`
`locals` for derived values — never expose one as an input
Never hardcode region, account ID, or environment
Backend and provider config belong to the root, not a child
`examples/` doubles as docs and as the integration target
`terraform-docs` builds the input table from descriptions
`create_x` booleans that toggle whole resources: n flags, 2^n plans
Nested `dynamic` blocks fed by nested objects — provider schema, rebuilt badly
`for_each` over keys computed from other resources: unknown keys break plan
`locals` longer than the resources they feed
An input named `overrides` or `extra_config` of type `any`
Wraps one resource and passes every argument through: that is a rename
Logic-to-resource ratio above ~1:1 means it became a program
The `any` escape hatch is the contract admitting defeat
Every conditional is a path nobody has ever applied
Combinations grow faster than your `examples/` directory
Untested paths surface as a surprise destroy at 2am

blocks.q: Should this input exist at all?
a_bullets: Readability: can a Terraform reader predict the plan from the call site?
Blast radius: can one input value destroy a database?
If yes to the second, that input should not exist

items: Do not extract a module until the third real caller
Two callers is coincidence, not a pattern
Copied HCL is cheap to delete; a bad module is load-bearing
Prefer duplication over the wrong abstraction

left.title: One `var.topology`
items: branches everywhere
plan varies wildly
read source to call

right.title: Two modules
items: `vpc_public`
`vpc_private`
predictable plan

blocks.title: Un-Abstracting
items: Inline the module back into the root
Delete the dead branches
Re-extract only what is truly shared

blocks.title: Counter-Balance
blocks.text: Too thin costs too. A module that only sets two defaults adds a layer of indirection for no leverage at all.

items: Module sources resolve before any expression is evaluated
Re-run `init` after adding or changing any module
Cyclic composition reports a cycle with no useful location

slides.page_title: When a Module Is Too Clever

items: `?ref=main` means your infra changes when a stranger merges
Unpinned registry module: a minor bump rewrites the plan in CI
Whole resource objects passed in couple you to provider schema
That schema changes next release, and your module goes with it
`sensitive = true` still lands plaintext in `terraform.tfstate`
And in provider debug logs when `TF_LOG` is on
`provider` block in a child blocks `for_each`, breaks removal, warns each plan
`terraform_remote_state` as a database creates hidden apply ordering
`terraform providers` and `terraform graph`
`terraform state list` and `terraform console`
`.terraform/modules/modules.json` for resolved paths
`moved` rewrites state addresses instead of recreating
Also the fix when you wrap a module in `count` after the fact
`removed` drops state only; `count = 0` really destroys

slides.page_title: Common Mistakes and How They Bite

blocks.title: Read The Plan
blocks.text: Nobody catches a destroy buried in 900 lines of nested module diff. Keep roots flat enough that the plan is actually read.
A module is a directory. Variables in, outputs out, nothing else is public — and pinning is your job, not Terraform's.

items: The last component is the one that floats
Semver: MAJOR removes an input, MINOR adds an optional one
Adding a required variable is breaking, though nothing was deleted
Pre-releases like `1.0.0-rc1` need an exact request

blocks.title: Upgrade Ritual
blocks.text: Bump one module version, run `terraform plan`, read the diff, then commit the pin. Never bulk-bump a whole root at once.

items: Sources decide where code comes from
Versions decide when it changes
There is no module lock file — only providers lock
Pin both in roots; float them in libraries
A module is a directory of `.tf` files — nothing more
Variables in, outputs out; nothing else is public
Everything flattens into one plan and one state file
Child addresses are prefixed: `module.vpc.aws_subnet.private[0]`
Output of one module into the input of the next
Terraform infers the whole graph from those references
`moved` blocks make restructuring non-destructive
The reference alone creates the edge — no `depends_on`
`depends_on` on a module waits for all of it, killing parallelism
Three levels deep and nobody reads the plan

blocks.title: Switching Costs
blocks.text: Moving a module from `count` to `for_each` re-creates everything unless you write `moved` blocks for each key first.

left.title: Design
items: one purpose
few required inputs
useful outputs
examples, docs, tags

right.title: Complexity
items: count booleans
count `dynamic`
locals vs resources
readability test

blocks.title: Style Picker
items: Encapsulation for opinionated app modules
Inversion of control for shared libraries
Concrete when you are unsure
Look up the VPC by tag at the caller instead
Beats threading one ID through four module levels
Fewer threaded inputs means fewer breaking renames
Rule of three before extraction, always
Duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction
You can abstract later; you cannot un-ship an interface

blocks.title: Final Measure
blocks.text: The best module is boring: predictable plan, obvious inputs. Measure it by how fast a new teammate calls it correctly without reading its source.

caption.text: Part 2 of TERRAFORM MODULES. Most Terraform pain is not the provider — it is a module with eleven booleans and no version pin. This handbook walks the whole contract: variables in, outputs out, where sources resolve, why `~> 3.1` and `~> 3.1.4` mean different things, and how `moved` blocks let you rename without a destroy. Ten pages, ending with the two checklists that tell you when a module got too clever to keep.
